sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Geographic Context**: The Singphos inhabited the **Hukawng Valley** and the **Patkai Range**, bordering Assam and Burma.
• **Primary Trigger**: The British occupation of Assam following the **Treaty of Yandabo (1826)**, which disrupted the traditional autonomy of the Singpho chiefs.
• **Nature of Resistance**: Primarily a **guerrilla-style warfare** aimed at reclaiming lost political authority and resisting the imposition of British revenue systems.
• **Key Metric / Factor**: The rebellion was not a single event but a sustained resistance spanning from **1830 to 1843**, characterized by multiple localized skirmishes.

items.title: Major Drivers of Rebellion
items.content:
• **Political**: Loss of traditional rights and interference in the selection of tribal chiefs.
• **Economic**: British attempts to control the tea-growing regions and trade routes.

items.title: Challenges & Way Forward
items.content:
• **Challenges**: Lack of unified pan-tribal leadership and superior British military technology (artillery).
• **Legacy**: The rebellion forced the British to adopt a 'Frontier Policy' involving a mix of military force and 'political pensions' to pacify tribal leaders.

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: Do not confuse the Singpho Rebellion with the Ahom Revolt. While both occurred in Assam, the Singphos were a distinct tribal group with different socio-political motivations.
Mains Value Addition: Use the term 'Frontier Imperialism' to describe the British response to the Singpho rebellion, highlighting the transition from trade-based interest to territorial control.

keyTakeaways: The Singpho Rebellion was a reaction to the post-1826 British expansion into Upper Assam.
It highlights the clash between traditional tribal autonomy and the centralized colonial administrative state.
The rebellion was eventually suppressed through a combination of military force and the co-option of tribal chiefs via political pensions.
